records.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
records.summary: São Tomé and Príncipe demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2012; small, peaceful, tourism-growing islands; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; thin community.

sources.claim: Everything Explained summary: legal since 2012; equal age of consent 18 since 2021 (Law 15/2021, previously 16); no relationship recognition or adoption; Labour Code 2019 Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation; no gender-identity recognition.

WIKI2 (Wikipedia mirror): LGBTQ rights in São Tomé and Príncipe - legal since 2012, sexual-orientation discrimination protections, no relationship recognition, no adoption, no military, no gender-identity recognition.

Alchetron (Wikipedia-derived): LGBT rights in São Tomé and Príncipe - same-sex activity legal under the 2012 Penal Code; age of consent 16 regardless of orientation (pre-2021); no relationship recognition; no discrimination protections (per this older snapshot); ICCPR signed 31 Oct 1995.

records.name: Suriname
records.summary:
Suriname demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal; the constitution's “any other status” clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination; and the 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act added employment protections. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but Paramaribo's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in Paramaribo; low tourist infrastructure generally.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 8.2 of the constitution prohibits discrimination including 'any other status' (argued to extend to SOGI); the 2022 Equal Treatment Labor Act explicitly bans SOGI discrimination at work; same-sex intercourse not criminalised; the penal code protects against hate speech; legal gender recognition advanced via the January 2022 appeals-court decision in De Staat Suriname v. Paris Yvanna Simson ordering registration changes for a trans woman.

Civil society report (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform Suriname) to the UN Human Rights Committee's 141st session (July 2024) on ICCPR implementation in Suriname - includes non-discrimination and gender-equality sections covering LGBT issues.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname: documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality, corruption, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities'.

LGBT Platform Suriname + Akahatá + Heartland Alliance stakeholder report (Oct 2015) to the Human Rights Committee: the March 2015 Penal Code revisions (Articles 175, 175a, 176) added sexual-orientation protections (1 year jail or fine for discrimination), but implementation lags; government members' anti-gay positions and media/music-industry hostility perpetuate homophobia.

UN Geneva meeting summary (July 2024): Human Rights Committee experts commended Suriname's commitment to judicial independence during its fourth ICCPR periodic-report review, asking about the National Human Rights Institute and indigenous rights.

Suriname LGBT Platform UPR pre-session summary (March 2016): since the 2011 UPR, Suriname equalised the age of consent and added discrimination provisions (2015); but the pension act excludes same-sex couples from survivor pensions contrary to the constitution's non-discrimination principle; the Platform has never been included in consultative processes.

records.name: Slovakia
records.summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveler-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues, EU free movement, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022, a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside Tepláreň, a Bratislava LGBT bar — classified as Slovakia's first modern terrorist attack. The state responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding: parliament advanced a bill to make legal gender recognition impossible (genetic-test-only basis), and constitutional amendments declaring gender immutable have been proposed. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in Bratislava.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against trans recognition.

sources.claim: Wikipedia article on the 2022 Bratislava shooting: a double murder outside the Tepláreň LGBT bar (12 October 2022), killing Juraj Vankulič and Matúš Horváth; the perpetrator's manifesto was anti-LGBT; classified as a homophobic hate crime/terrorism; domestic and international reactions.

BIRN/Balkan Insight (Feb 2023): in the shadow of the attack, the situation of Slovakia's trans community remains precarious - long subjected to harmful practices including forced sterilisation (required for document changes), trans people remain a political target even after the terrorist attack on the LGBT bar.

Amnesty International (May 2023): the Slovak parliament should reject a bill making legal gender recognition impossible - trans people have been able to access LGR in Slovakia for more than 40 years, and the bill would remove this right in breach of international human-rights obligations.

Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Dunja Mijatović's letter (April 2023) to the Slovak National Council: six months after the Tepláreň attack, no discernible progress; human rights of LGBTI people appear more, not less, at risk; concerned about regressive legislative proposals including the LGR ban bill.

Pew Research Center (Oct 2018): 'Eastern and Western Europeans Differ on Importance of Religion, Views of Minorities, and Key Social Issues' - fewer Central and Eastern Europeans (including Slovaks) would extend marriage to gay or lesbian couples - comparative attitude data.

records.name: Slovenia
records.summary:
Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government.

No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): one of the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe - comprehensive anti-discrimination law since 2016 (Protection Against Discrimination Act, Advocate of the Principle of Equality); first post-Communist country to legalise same-sex marriage (2022 Constitutional Court ruling; effective January 2023 with joint adoption); legal gender recognition possible but lacks a clear, modern legal framework.
F&M Global Barometers country profile for Slovenia: composite LGBT-rights perception scores including the Global Barometer of Transgender Rights index.

Slovenian Ministry of the Interior (Oct 2022): terminated local jurisdiction in gender-change procedures - trans people no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of their trans identity in their local environment; procedures may now take place at any administrative unit; 157 gender reassignments entered in the civil register since 2005 (31 in 2022).

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Slovenia: police failed to intervene in attacks around the Pride march and discouraged reporting; Legebitra documented 17 cases and TransAkcija 25 cases of direct bias-motivated speech in 2023; an emergency parliamentary meeting concluded the ministry should adopt a national action plan.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Slovenia: courts recognised LGBTI asylum seekers' vulnerabilities; a journalist was ruled to have violated the journalists' code for portraying gender reassignment as commercialised and harmful; SDS and NSi proposed criminalising 'promotion' of homosexuality/trans identities (up to 3 years) mirroring Hungary/Russia laws - swiftly rejected by the government; a magazine special edition pushed anti-trans narratives; NSi proposed removing gender-affirming surgery from health coverage.
US State Department 2023 Human Rights Practices report for Slovenia (archived): official assessment including treatment of LGBTI persons.

Peace Institute ENACT national report (Jan 2025): 'Enhancing the capacity of civil society organisations to support victims of anti-LGBTQI hate crimes' - Slovenia's legal and political context on anti-LGBTI hate crimes, part of an EU-funded six-country project.

B92 (July 2006): Slovenia passed a same-sex marriage law but with restrictions - ceremonies limited to the two partners and a registration official, no friends or relatives, only in a state office; gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the step but criticised the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

records.name: Sweden
records.summary:
Sweden is very safe. A new Legal Gender Recognition Act (July 2025) simplified the procedure and separated it from surgery requirements, but it still falls short of self-determination — a medical examination and a decision by the National Board of Health and Welfare are required. Sweden was the last Nordic country to reform its 1972-era LGR law.

One documented axis-C friction: the Medley swimming-pool company's national guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports, and the government is mapping digital threats against LGBTQI individuals. There are no documented severe incidents (no tourist-rape, mob violence, or Pride-terrorism equivalent to Norway's Oslo shooting). Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, and there is no criminalisation or rollback movement.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Library of Congress entry (April 2024) covers Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU (July 2025): Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act took effect 1 July 2025 - it simplifies the procedure (digital healthcare consultations, age limit lowered to 16, parental consent under 16) but falls short of self-determination: a medical examination and a National Board of Health and Welfare decision are still required, continuing to pathologise trans people; the Christian Democrats and right-wing opposition vow to reverse it.

SVT (Oct 2025, in Swedish): swimming-pool giant Medley stops trans people from choosing changing rooms - the company motivates its policy as being 'for all visitors to feel safe', a policy affecting trans swimmers' access to facilities.

Brå (Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13 summary: 'Persons suspected of offences with LGBTQI-related hate crimes' - descriptive analysis of suspects in reported offences with identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives, supplementing Sweden's hate-crime statistics.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Sweden: Stockholm's second LGBTI senior residence opened; the Migration Agency was instructed to improve consistency in LGBTI asylum claims and conversion-practices cases, though RFSL reports continued reliance on stereotypical credibility assessments; asylum and migration legislation tightening, with concerns it may disproportionately affect LGBTI asylum seekers.

Sundevall & Persson, 'LGBT in the Military: Policy Development in Sweden 1944-2014' (Sexuality Research and Social Policy, 2016): archival study of Swedish Armed Forces LGBT policy - two 'turns' (1971-79, when homosexuality was classified as mental illness and framed as a security/blackmail risk, and 2000-09, shifting focus to organisational structures); no formal ban ever existed.
Newsweek (2019): Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations in the Spartacus Gay Travel Index - Sweden's top-tier ranking for LGBT travellers.
The Local (Jan 2017): Sweden to stop classifying transgender people as 'mentally ill' - the National Board of Health and Welfare (Socialstyrelsen) announced the change, widely criticised as overdue.

records.name: Eswatini
records.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): common law criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy; no legal gender recognition and limited gender-affirming healthcare; intersex people lack safeguards; in April 2022 the High Court rejected ESGM's bid for registration, but in June 2023 the Supreme Court declared the Registrar's decision void; the Ministry of Commerce still refuses registration, claiming the NGO's name and objectives 'seek to offend against customary principles'.
Freedom House 2024 for Eswatini: 'Not Free' (17/100) - an absolute monarchy; political dissent harshly punished; discrimination against women and LGBT+ people among the human-rights problems.
BTI 2024 Country Report Eswatini (Bertelsmann): the last absolute monarchy in Africa - the King and Queen Mother hold veto powers over all branches of government; governance and human-rights context.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Eswatini: official assessment - sodomy laws (common law) remain; significant societal stigma; no legal protections for LGBT persons.

Swazi Media Commentary (Dec 2018): a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in Coates Valley; Rock of Hope's Melusi Simelane welcomed it while noting religious hate speech; a Gender Links report described a meeting where 20+ pastors called LGBTI behaviour 'demonic' and refused to let gay people 'flaunt' themselves.

Mambaonline (July 2018): history made as the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect' success - more than 2,000 people attended in Mbabane, with a police-escorted march around Prince of Wales Stadium; organiser Melusi Simelane of Rock of Hope was 'beyond thrilled'.

Mambaonline (July 2019): Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities (ESGM), calling its objectives a 'negative mindset' - other groups had to include 'acceptable' health/HIV aims to register; ESGM's first objective is to advance LGBT rights.

records.name: Seychelles
records.summary: Seychelles is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.

sources.claim: Cornell Law School gender-justice page for Seychelles: the constitution guarantees fundamental rights - Article 16 prohibits torture, Article 27 affirms equal protection and prohibits discrimination including on sex; same-sex conduct was decriminalised in Seychelles in 2016.

PinkNews (May 2016): Seychelles repealed the colonial-era Section 151 (up to 14 years for male same-sex 'unnatural offences') via the Penal Code (Amendment) Bill 2016 - the president had highlighted the need to abolish criminalising provisions; tourism (~20% of GDP) had been a 'no-go' area for LGBT tourism.
Queer In The World: 'LGBT Rights In Seychelles: Everything You Should Know Before You Visit' - country guide covering the legal situation and travel considerations.

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2024): 'Formerly an anti-gay haven, Seychelles becomes a protector of its LGBTQ citizens' - the new Penal Code (Amendment) Bill (18-8) increases sentences for hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability; HDT: after South Africa, the second African country protecting against all forms of hate-based victimisation.

records.name: Syria
records.summary:
Syria is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.

sources.claim: NOTE: The Guardians of the Gem report on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall of the Assad regime (April 2025) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).
EUAA Syria Country Focus, section 2.8.2: treatment of LGBTIQ persons by state, non-state and societal actors.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Articles 520 and 517 criminalise 'sexual acts against nature' and public indecency; no legal gender recognition and no prohibition of nonconsensual intersex interventions; during the 2011-2024 conflict, violence on SOGI grounds escalated - Islamist groups executed and publicly tortured sexual and gender minorities (particularly queer men and trans women); government forces arrested people on morality charges, committed enforced disappearances and sexual violence in detention.
HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Syria's Article 520 criminalisation and the situation of LGBT Syrians amid the conflict.

Syria Direct (Oct 2020): 'At home and abroad, LGBT Syrians fight to have their voices heard' - Amira al-Tabbaa's activism since 2004 helping those kicked out of work or home; in 'gay-friendly' Damascus cafes friends spoke 'only in whispers'; 'We need to break the door of the closet that they put us into and get out: We deserve life.'

Newsweek (2015): two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever UN Security Council meeting on LGBT rights (closed session, co-sponsored by the US and Chile) about constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews (June 2010): Syrian authorities raided private gay parties, arresting over 25 men - charged with 'homosexual acts', drugs, or 'obscene' parties; families refused to pay bail; police monitor cruising areas; Gay Middle East called for repeal of the 'antiquated' Article 520 of the 1949 Penal Code.
